Sources are the Wikipedia century and subject pages fetched in this session, with Britannica, National Geographic, PBS NOVA, Royal Museums Greenwich and the Harry Ransom Center where reached; the shared web-search budget ran out mid-session, so most tier-1 rows rest on two Wikipedia pages rather than Britannica.

events.t: The dog is domesticated in Siberia about 23,000 years ago.
The earliest pottery is made in China between about 20,000 and 16,000 years ago, long before farming.

On a creek near Puerto Montt in southern Chile, people build about twelve huts of wood and hide around 14,500 years ago, butcher mastodon-like Notiomastodon, gather nine kinds of seaweed and some 45 food plants, and leave a footprint. Tom Dillehay’s excavations from 1977 undermined the idea that the Clovis people came first; a 2026 study disputes the date and Dillehay contests it.

The Clovis culture spreads across North America, from southern Canada to northern Mexico, about 13,050–12,750 years ago. Its fluted stone points, named from Blackwater Draw near Clovis, New Mexico, tip the spears of mammoth and bison hunters; the genome of the Anzick child, buried in Montana with Clovis tools, ties them to today’s Native Americans.

events.n: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
events.t: Agriculture begins in the Fertile Crescent between about 10,000 and 9000 BC; sheep, then goats and cattle, are domesticated in South-west Asia in the same millennium.

events.fig: nearly 200 pillars in at least 20 enclosures
events.t: Hunter-gatherers raise great circular enclosures of carved T-shaped pillars on a hilltop near Şanlıurfa from about 9500 BC: foxes, boars, snakes and vultures are cut in the stone, and nearly 200 pillars may stand in at least 20 enclosures. Excavated by Klaus Schmidt from 1995, it is among the first monumental architecture made by human hands, perhaps older than farming itself.

Natufian hunters camp at the spring of Jericho around 10,000 BC and the first permanent settlement grows there between 9500 and 9000 BC. Around 8000 BC its people build a stone wall over 3.6 m high and a tower over 8.5 m high with 22 steps inside; in the later town, founded around 6800 BC, they plaster and paint the skulls of their dead.
Rice is domesticated in China between about 9000 and 6000 BC; by 5000 BC the Hemudu culture grows it in eastern China.
The potato is domesticated between about 8000 and 5000 BC in southern Peru and north-western Bolivia, around Lake Titicaca.

Çatalhöyük on the Konya plain flourishes around 7000 BC: houses packed wall to wall, entered by ladders through the roofs, which serve as streets. Its people paint murals and make more than 2,500 clay figurines; recent work puts the population at 600–800 in an average year, far below the early guesses of 5,000–7,000.

Maize is domesticated from the wild grass teosinte in southern Mexico, probably in the Balsas valley, about 9,000 years ago, and only once. It reaches highland Ecuador by 8,000 years ago; the oldest cobs, from Guilá Naquitz in Oaxaca, are about 6,250 years old.
Pottery from Mesopotamia shows boats with sails around 5500 BC; ancient Egypt follows.
Around 5400 BC the Ubaid people at Eridu in southern Iraq begin to farm grain in the arid south, and Uruk is founded around 5000 BC; the Choga Mami canals irrigate fields around 4700 BC.
The Vinča culture of the Balkans makes the earliest known copper smelting of the Old World; the timeline of inventions dates it to about 5000 BC in Serbia.

events.n: The stone circle of Nabta Playa
events.t: Herders at Nabta Playa in the Egyptian desert raise stone circles aligned to the summer solstice around 4800 BC.
Maize is farmed at Huaca Prieta on the north coast of Peru around 4700 BC, and the earliest known dyed cotton cloth, about 6,000 years old, is woven there.
The Varna culture of Bulgaria, from about 4600 to 4200 BC, buries its chiefs in graves of gold and shows the first signs of kingship.
Around 4000 BC the rock painters of Arnhem Land in northern Australia depict skirmishes between groups.

Bronze smelting begins in the fourth millennium BC; the Maykop culture of the Caucasus, of 3700–3000 BC, may be its origin, and the earliest bronze swords, of arsenical bronze, come from Arslantepe in Anatolia around 3300 BC.
Silk garments are made in China by 3630 BC.
The megalithic temples of Ġgantija on Gozo, in Malta, are begun around 3600 BC.

The Norte Chico civilisation of northern Peru begins around 3600 BC; large-scale settlement and communal building start at Caral-Supe around 3100 BC, and the oldest adobe building of the Americas is raised in Peru.
Horses are probably domesticated on the Eurasian steppe around 3500 BC; the Botai culture of northern Kazakhstan has the evidence.
Around 3500 BC the drying of the Sahara spurs the Neolithic of the Sahel; in Egypt the dead are already being mummified at Nekhen.

events.fig: the oldest wheel, about 5,150 years old
events.t: Evidence of the wheel appears between about 4000 and 3400 BC in Ukraine, Poland and Germany. The oldest wooden wheel yet found, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, is about 5,150 years old; the potter’s wheel is in use in Mesopotamia by 3250 BC.
Ötzi dies in the Ötztal Alps around 3300 BC, it is believed by homicide.
Camels are domesticated around 3000 BC, and the first agriculture appears in North Africa.
The Cycladic civilisation and the Aegean Bronze Age begin around 3000 BC; the marble Harp Player of Keros is made around 2800–2700 BC.
Jawa in the Jordanian desert is founded around 3000 BC with the world’s first known dam.

Before 3000 BC the Liangzhu culture of the lower Yangtze carves deity images on jade cong. Near Eastern grains appear in China around 3000 BC and the potter’s wheel is in use there in the third millennium BC.
The shekel is introduced in Mesopotamia as a unit of weight and money; the Sumerians build cities and work metals, and gold comes into use in the Middle East.
Stonehenge is begun around 3000 BC: its first phase is a ditch and bank with 56 wooden posts. Newgrange in Ireland is built between about 3000 and 2500 BC.
The rock engravings of the Sydney region date from around 3000 BC.

events.n: The first pottery of the Americas
events.t: The first pottery of the Americas is made in what is now Ecuador in the third millennium BC, while settled villages spread through Mesoamerica.
By Manfred Korfmann’s reading of the excavations, Troy is founded around 2920 BC.
The wide-eyed votive statues of the Square Temple at Eshnunna are made around 2900 BC, as the Early Dynastic period of Sumer begins.
The first kingdom of Mari on the Euphrates is founded around 2900 BC.
From about 2900 BC Sumerian pictographs evolve into phonograms, signs for sounds; the first Akkadian names are recorded around 2890 BC.
Hotepsekhemwy begins Egypt’s Second Dynasty around 2890 BC, and wars divide the kingdom from 2775 to 2650 BC.
By Vietnamese tradition Kinh Dương Vương founds the Hồng Bàng dynasty and the kingdom of Xích Quỷ in 2879 BC.
Egypt installs a calendar of 365 days around 2874 BC.
A bristlecone pine germinates in the White Mountains of California around 2832 BC: the Methuselah tree.
The kingdom of Elam is created in south-western Iran around 2800–2700 BC.
The Harappan 2 phase of the Indus valley, around 2800–2600 BC, leads to the unified Indus civilisation of about 2600 BC.
A ploughed field at Kalibangan in the Indus valley is dated to about 2800 BC; the first ploughs had been made in Europe by 3500 BC.
A Cycladic sculptor carves the marble Seated Harp Player of Keros around 2800–2700 BC.
The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture of Romania, Moldova and south-western Ukraine ends around 2750 BC.
The first Egyptian statuary, shale and limestone figures of King Khasekhemwy, is made at Nekhen around 2700 BC.
Chinese tradition dates the mythical reign of the Yellow Emperor from about 2698 BC; the age of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors is counted from 2852 BC.
Imhotep builds the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara in the twenty-seventh century BC, Egypt’s earliest building of stone.
Egypt develops copper mines and turquoise quarries in Sinai under Sneferu and Khufu; the earliest African picture of ploughing is painted in the tomb of Itet and Nefermaat at Meidum.
Sneferu’s armies bring back about 7,000 prisoners from Nubia and 11,000 prisoners and 13,100 cattle from Libya; he sends 40 ships to Byblos for cedar, and copper and turquoise are mined in Sinai.
The semi-legendary Gilgamesh is supposed to reign at Uruk around 2650 BC; Nippur keeps a bronze bar that defines the cubit.
The Harappan town of Kalibangan is abandoned around 2650 BC as the Ghaggar river dries; at Dholavira reservoirs, script, metals and pottery are in use.

Caral in Peru’s Supe valley is inhabited from about 2600 to 2000 BC, its temple pyramid 150 m long and 28 m high. With some 3,000 people, and perhaps 20,000 across the nineteen other temple sites of the valley, its excavators call it the oldest urban centre of the Americas; a knotted cord found there may be a quipu.
The Early Minoan I period of Crete runs from about 2600 to 2400 BC.
The Copper Age settlements of Los Millares and Zambujal are founded in Iberia around 2600 BC.
The Instructions of Shuruppak, among the earliest known literary texts, are composed in Sumer in 2600–2500 BC.
The Royal Cemetery of Ur is built in the twenty-sixth century BC; under Mesannepada, from about 2560 BC, Ur grows into a major capital.
Khufu reigns from about 2551 to 2526 BC and builds the Great Pyramid of Giza; his son Khafre adds his pyramid and the Great Sphinx. Djedefre is the first pharaoh to call himself Son of Ra.

events.n: The war of Lagash and Umma
events.t: The border dispute between Lagash and Umma begins around 2550 BC, under Mesilim of Kish.
Assyria is established around 2500 BC; archaeology shows the site of Assur occupied by 2400 BC.
The Sumerians harness domestic donkeys to war chariots in the twenty-fifth century BC.
The archive of Ebla in Syria is written between about 2500 and 2250 BC, while scribal schools flourish in Sumer.
Work on the underground Hypogeum of Ħal Saflieni in Malta begins around 2500 BC.
The earliest surviving ski is left in a bog at Hoting in Sweden in the twenty-fifth century BC.
The pyramid of Khafre is built at Giza around 2500 BC, with the seated statue Khafre Enthroned. In the next dynasty the Seated Scribe is carved at Saqqara.
Mohenjo-daro grows to about 18 km² and 20,000–50,000 people between 2500 and 2000 BC. The Indus civilisation at its peak covers about 480,000 km².

events.n: The fishing towns of the Peruvian coast
events.t: Around 2500 BC the people of the Peruvian coast live on fish and mussels, and long-distance trade routes cross South America.
Rice is first introduced to Malaysia around 2500 BC.
Skara Brae in Orkney is abandoned around 2500 BC after about 600 years of occupation.
Egypt gives the first official mention of beekeeping and the first documented courier service for written documents in the twenty-fourth century BC.
Stonehenge is built between about 2400 and 2200 BC, as the megalithic culture spreads through Europe and the western Mediterranean.
The first written Akkadian, the Semitic language of Sargon’s empire, survives from the twenty-fourth century BC.
Hekla in Iceland erupts around 2360 BC, the eruption known as Hekla 4.
Lugal-Zage-Si of Umma conquers Gu-Edin and unites Sumer around 2350 BC; Mari is destroyed for the first time.
Unas, the last king of the Fifth Dynasty, dies around 2345 BC and the Sixth Dynasty begins with Teti.
Korean myth has Dangun found Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, in 2333 BC.
Egyptians widen a branch of the Nile into the Bahr Yusuf canal to Lake Moeris around 2300 BC.
The Únětice culture emerges in today’s Czech Republic around 2300 BC, as metals come into use in northern Europe.
Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon-god Nanna at Ur, is born around 2285 BC; her alabaster disc is made there.
The victory stela of Naram-Sin of Akkad is carved around 2254–2218 BC, probably at Sippar; it is later carried off to Susa.
Maize, domesticated in southern Mexico, is cultivated in Central America by around 2250 BC, and its farming begins in New Mexico and Arizona about 4,100 years ago.
Around 2240 BC Akkad passes Memphis as the largest city in the world.
By one estimate migrants from India reach Australia around 2218 BC and mix with the Indigenous Australians.
Nomads invade Akkad from 2217 to 2193 BC, and around 2180 BC the Akkadian Empire falls to the Gutians.
Austronesian seafarers reach the Batanes Islands of the northern Philippines around 2200 BC.
Iron is smelted at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Anatolia between about 2200 and 2000 BC.
From about 2200 to 2100 BC a great aridification, the 4.2-kiloyear event, strikes Africa and Asia, and the states of the Old World collapse.

events.n: The end of the Old Kingdom
events.t: Pepi II may die around 2184 BC after the longest reign in history, 94 years. By 2181 BC the Old Kingdom of Egypt has ended and the First Intermediate Period begins.
The city-state of Lagash is re-established around 2150 BC, while the Gutians hold Akkad; the Middle Minoan period begins on Crete around 2160 BC.
Gudea rules Lagash from about 2144 to 2124 BC; his votive statues survive.
Ur-Nammu campaigns across Sumer from 2112 BC and founds the Third Dynasty of Ur; the Ziggurat of Ur is built. In 2004 BC the Elamites sack Ur and the dynasty ends.
The Sumerian epic poems, Gilgamesh among them, are written between about 2100 and 2000 BC; an Akkadian version follows.
Shahr-e Sukhteh, the Burnt City of eastern Persia, is abandoned in the twenty-first century BC.
The Sintashta culture emerges on the northern Eurasian steppe around 2100 BC.
The inner bluestone circles of Stonehenge are raised in the twenty-first century BC. Seahenge, on the Norfolk shore, is built in the late spring of 2049 BC.

events.n: Yu the Great and the Xia
events.t: By tradition Yu the Great founds the Xia dynasty in China around 2070 BC; a great flood in the Jishi gorge around 1920 BC may lie behind the legend.
The Middle Kerma culture begins in Upper Nubia around 2050 BC.
Mentuhotep II of Thebes completes the reunification of Egypt around 2040 BC, and the Middle Kingdom begins.
Early bronze objects at Ban Chiang in Thailand date from around 2000 BC, from a society without cities or armies.
The Capacha culture begins in Colima, in western Mexico, around 2000 BC, and people settle at Matanchén in Nayarit.
Glass appears around 2000 BC, and Old Assyrian cuneiform evolves from the Sumerian.
Farmers and herders settle in what is now Kenya around 2000 BC, and the ancestors of the Latins arrive in Italy.
The last woolly mammoths die out on Wrangel Island in the Arctic around 2000 BC, centuries after the pyramids of Giza were built.
Amenemhat I founds the Twelfth Dynasty around 1995 BC. Senusret I conquers Lower Nubia to the Second Cataract in 1953 BC, and war with Nubia follows in 1913–1903 BC.
A chieftain, the King of Leubingen, is buried in Thuringia in 1942 BC under a stone cairn 20 m across.
A great flood bursts from the Jishi gorge on the upper Yellow River around 1920 BC; it may be linked with the founding of the Xia dynasty.
Around 1900 BC the Mokaya of the Pacific coast of Chiapas, in Mexico, are preparing drinks of cacao.
The late Harappan phase of the Indus civilisation begins around 1900 BC, and its port of Lothal in Gujarat is abandoned.
The Old Palace period of Minoan Crete begins around 1900 BC, and the palace at Knossos rises.
The last Sumerian dynasty falls around 1900 BC; the Amorite Shamshi-Adad I founds a kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia around 1808 BC.
Senusret III of Egypt’s Middle Kingdom inspects the Nubian frontier around 1860 BC and leads four punitive campaigns south. A head of him is now at the Nelson-Atkins Museum.
The first alphabet, the Proto-Sinaitic script, appears in Egypt around 1850 BC.
The Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus, written around 1825 BC at el-Lahun, is the oldest known Egyptian medical text.
From about 1800 BC the Hyksos settle in the Nile delta with their capital at Avaris, and by about 1750 BC they hold northern Egypt.
Settled Maya communities form in Mesoamerica around 1800 BC.
The Nordic Bronze Age begins in Scandinavia around 1800 BC.
The sixth city of Troy flourishes for five centuries, from about 1800 to 1300 BC.
Hammurabi of Babylon sacks Mari in 1757 BC and destroys the palace of its king Zimri-Lim.
Mount Veniaminof on the Alaska Peninsula erupts colossally around 1750 BC.

events.n: The end of the Indus cities
events.t: The Indus Valley civilisation declines from about 1800 BC and ends around 1700 BC; the Cemetery H culture carries it on.
Around 1700 BC the Old Palace period of Crete ends and the second palaces are built; Aegean metalworkers now make ornaments to rival the Near East’s jewellers.
Leavened bread is developed in Egypt around 1680 BC.
Around 1650 BC the Hyksos take Memphis; Egypt’s 13th and 14th dynasties collapse and the Hyksos 15th dynasty rules the north.
By tradition Tang of Shang overthrows Jie, the last king of Xia, at the battle of Mingtiao around 1646 BC or earlier, and establishes the Shang dynasty.
Tree rings across the world record a cooling of several years from 1627 BC, possibly from volcanic eruptions.
A pyramid is raised at El Morro del Tulcán, at today’s Popayán in Colombia, around 1600 BC.
Early Mycenaean culture, with its weapons, Cyclopean walls and chariots, appears around 1600 BC; by 1550 BC Mycenae dominates Achaea.

events.n: The rubber balls of El Manatí
events.t: A dozen rubber balls from the Olmec spring of El Manatí date to 1600 BC or earlier, made from latex mixed with the juice of a vine. They are older than the first known ballcourt, at Paso de la Amada around 1400 BC.
Babylonian astronomers record the appearances of Venus over 21 years on the Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa.
The Hittite king Mursili I sacks Babylon in 1595 BC. The First Dynasty of Babylon, Hammurabi’s, ends and the Kassites take Babylonia.
Ahmose I is crowned around 1550 BC and founds the 18th dynasty; the New Kingdom of Egypt begins.
Egypt conquers Nubia and the Levant in 1504–1492 BC.
A meteorite strikes Saaremaa in Estonia around 1500 BC and forms the Kaali crater.
The early traces of Maya civilisation, in Belize, date from around 1500 BC; the earliest traces of the Olmec are of the same century.
The early hymns of the Rigveda are dated by many scholars to around 1500 BC, in the Punjab.
One tradition puts the birth of Zoroaster, the prophet of the Iranian faith, around 1500 BC.
Hatshepsut is succeeded by Thutmose III around 1480 BC, and Egypt reaches its greatest extent; around 1469 BC he defeats the Canaanites at Megiddo.
The Shang capital at Ao is walled in the fifteenth century BC with ramparts about 20 m wide at the base.
Mycenaeans conquer Crete around 1420 BC; the first Linear B tablets are written and the Palace of Minos burns around 1400 BC.
The ballcourt of Paso de la Amada is built around 1400 BC; the Olmec rubber balls of El Manatí are older still.
Ugarit on the Syrian coast is at its height from about 1400 to 1250 BC; its texts attest a written alphabet.
Šuppiluliuma I leads the Hittite Empire to its peak around 1380–1336 BC and conquers the weakened Mitanni; Assyria frees itself under Ashur-uballit I.
Akhenaten builds a new capital, Akhetaten, at Amarna in 1372–1350 BC. Tutankhamun dies around 1325 BC and is buried in the Valley of the Kings.
Large public buildings are raised at San Lorenzo in Mexico between 1350 and 1250 BC.
Between about 1350 and 1250 BC pastoral nomadism develops on the Central Asian steppes, with cattle herded on horseback.
A merchant ship sinks off Uluburun, south of Kaş, around 1320–1295 BC, carrying the trade of the Late Bronze Age Mediterranean.
The pharaohs of the 19th dynasty complete their temples at Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel in the thirteenth century BC.
The Lion Gate and the Treasury of Atreus are built at Mycenae in the thirteenth century BC, and the palace scribes of Pylos write Linear B.
Around 1300 BC the Shang settle their capital at Yin, Anyang, where they flourish until 1046 BC. Their armies are organised in companies of a hundred men and sections of five chariots.

events.n: The Battle of the Ten Kings
events.t: Around 1300 BC, by the Rigveda, King Sudas defeats a coalition of ten kings in the north-west of India.

events.n: The battle in the Tollense valley
events.t: Some 4,000 men fight at a causeway over the Tollense in northern Germany in the thirteenth century BC, the largest known prehistoric battle north of the Alps.
Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittites fight at Kadesh on the Orontes in 1274 BC; neither wins outright, and both sides lose heavily.
Lapita pottery at Bourewa, on the south-west coast of Viti Levu in Fiji, is dated to about 1260 BC: the seafarers of the Lapita culture have crossed the open sea to Fiji.
From about 1250 BC the Urnfield culture, burning its dead and burying the ashes in urns, marks the Late Bronze Age of central and western Europe.

events.n: The Phoenicians in the far west
events.t: The Phoenicians found a port at Lisbon around 1200 BC and Gadir, Cádiz, around 1104 BC, beyond the Pillars of Hercules.

The Olmec civilisation develops on the Gulf coast of Mexico around 1200 BC, with its first great centre at San Lorenzo until about 900 BC. Its seventeen known colossal heads, thought to be rulers, weigh up to an estimated 25–55 tonnes; the best jade comes from the Motagua valley of Guatemala.
Greek tradition dates the fall of Troy to the Mycenaeans to 24 April 1184 BC, after a ten-year war that legend begins around 1194 BC.
Hittite power collapses around 1180 BC and Hattusa is destroyed; the last Kassite king of Babylon falls to the Elamites the same year.

events.n: Ramesses III and the Sea Peoples
events.t: In the eighth year of his reign, about 1177 BC, Ramesses III repels the Sea Peoples from Egypt.
Pharaoh Ramesses V dies of smallpox in 1160 BC.
The Hekla 3 eruption in Iceland in 1159 BC triggers eighteen years of cooling.
The Cascajal block, of about 1100–900 BC, carries 62 signs, 28 of them distinct, and may be writing; many scholars doubt it because it was found out of context.
Around 1100 BC Mycenaean civilisation ends and the Greek Dark Ages begin; the Dorians are supposed to invade.
The earliest evidence of farming in the highlands of Kenya dates from the eleventh century BC.
Ramesses XI dies in 1069 BC and the 20th dynasty ends; Smendes founds the 21st.
The Bamboo Annals record five planets gathering in the evening sky in May 1059 BC, thirteen years before the Zhou overthrow the Shang.
The Phoenician alphabet is invented in the eleventh century BC, about when the Latins arrive in Italy.
Saul becomes the first king of the Israelites around 1026 BC; David succeeds around 1010 BC.
The earliest extant written Aramaic dates from the late tenth century BC; around 500 BC Darius I makes Aramaic the official language of the western Persian Empire.
Bronze Age goldsmiths of Central Europe make the ceremonial golden hats in the late tenth century BC.

events.n: The Iron Age kingdoms of India
events.t: Around 1000 BC Iron Age kingdoms rule northern and southern India: Kuru, Panchala, Kosala, Videha and the Pandya.
The Latins arrive in Italy around 1000 BC, in the age of the Villanovan culture.
The Sa Huỳnh culture begins in central and southern Vietnam around 1000 BC.

David, king of the united monarchy of Israel, dies around 965 BC. By tradition Solomon completes the First Temple in Jerusalem in 957 BC; after his death in 931 BC the kingdom splits into Judah and Israel.
Sparta is founded late in the tenth century BC, in Greece’s dark age; the Lefkandi centaur is made on Euboea.
Shoshenq I founds Egypt’s 22nd dynasty around 943 BC, at the end of the 21st.
Anuradhapura is founded in Sri Lanka around 900 BC; in northern Italy the Villanovan culture emerges.

The Chavín culture of the Peruvian Andes develops around 900 BC around its temple at Chavín de Huántar, built in at least fifteen phases; at its heart stands the Lanzón, a carved granite shaft 4.53 m tall showing a fanged god. Chavín style spreads from Piura to Paracas before the culture ends around 250 BC.

events.n: La Venta and the Olmec pyramids
events.t: La Venta is the main Olmec centre from about 900 to 400 BC, with its Great Pyramid; around 800 BC the Olmecs are building pyramids. In the north-eastern woodlands of North America the Adena culture appears.
Ashurnasirpal II becomes king of Assyria in 884 BC and moves his capital to Nimrud around 880 BC.
The kingdom of Urartu is unified around 860 BC in the Armenian highlands; Argishti I founds Erebuni, today’s Yerevan, in 782 BC.

Shalmaneser III of Assyria fights a coalition led by Damascus at Qarqar on the Orontes in 854 or 853 BC, without a decision; in 842 BC he devastates Damascus and Israel and the Phoenician cities pay him tribute.
By tradition Abhiyaza founds the Tagaung kingdom on the Irrawaddy in northern Burma around 850 BC.

events.n: The first year of Chinese annual dating
events.t: King Li of Zhou is driven into exile in 841 BC; from that year Chinese history is dated year by year without a break.
Around 800 BC the Iron Age and the Hallstatt culture spread through Central Europe with the Proto-Celtic language; the Etruscan civilisation emerges in Italy.

events.n: The iron port of Sungai Batu
events.t: A port and iron-working centre is founded at Sungai Batu in Kedah on the Malay Peninsula around 788 BC.
Hao is sacked in 771 BC and King You is killed; the Western Zhou ends and the court moves east to Chengzhou in 770 BC. The Spring and Autumn period begins in 722 BC.
The Iliad and the Odyssey are dated to 750–650 BC, the age of the first Olympiads and the Greek alphabet.
Tiglath-Pileser III takes the Assyrian throne in 745 BC and makes Israel pay tribute. Sargon II conquers the kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and founds a new capital at Dur-Sharrukin in 717 BC.
Corinth founds Syracuse in Sicily in 734 BC and Sparta founds Taras in 706 BC; the Greek colonies of the west begin.
Piye, king of Kush at Napata since about 730 BC, invades Egypt in 728 BC, takes Memphis and founds the 25th dynasty.
The Upanishads are composed in India around 700 BC. On the Pontic steppe the Scythians begin to settle the lands of the Cimmerians.
An inscription of the 690s BC from D’mt in Ethiopia names Karib’il Watar, king of Saba in Arabia, across the Red Sea.
Taharqa of Kush takes the Egyptian throne around 690 BC, one of the Nubian pharaohs of the 25th dynasty; his sphinx is carved at Kawa. He holds off the first Assyrian invasion in 674 BC.
Esarhaddon invades Egypt in 671 BC and takes Memphis; Ashurbanipal sacks Thebes in 664 BC. Psamtik I drives the Assyrians out and by 656 BC rules all Egypt; the Kushite dynasty ends.
Nineveh becomes the largest city in the world in 668 BC. In the 640s BC Ashurbanipal founds there the library that keeps the earliest complete copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh.
By tradition colonists from Megara under Byzas found Byzantium on the Bosporus in 667 BC, the century of Greek colonies from Abdera to Cyrene.
Japanese tradition dates the founding of the country by Emperor Jimmu to 11 February 660 BC.
The Lydians of western Anatolia strike the first metal coins in the seventh century BC; the timeline of inventions puts coinage at about 600 BC, in Lydia or Phoenicia.
The Zapotec civilisation begins to develop in the Valley of Oaxaca in the seventh century BC. In the Maya lowlands Piedras Negras is first occupied in the 650s BC.
Greek colonists found Cyrene in Libya around 631 BC.
Necho II of Egypt kills Josiah of Judah at Megiddo in 609 BC; at Carchemish in 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar defeats Necho.

events.n: The sixteen great states of India
events.t: Around 600 BC sixteen Mahajanapadas, the great realms, rule northern India. Pataliputra is established as a capital of Magadha around 500 BC, and Vaishali is counted the first republic.
Greeks from Phocaea found Massalia, Marseille, around 600 BC; Celts found Milan about the same time.
Solon reforms the laws of Athens in 594 BC. The tyrant Hippias is expelled in 510 BC and Cleisthenes’ reforms of 507–501 BC found the Athenian democracy.
An Egyptian army sacks Napata in 590 BC and the Kushite court moves south to Meroë on the Nile.

events.n: The Temple destroyed and the exile
events.t: Babylon takes Jerusalem in 597 BC and again in 587 BC; Solomon’s Temple is destroyed and the Babylonian captivity begins. After Cyrus takes Babylon the exiles may return, and the Second Temple is completed on 12 March 515 BC.
Thales of Miletus predicts the solar eclipse of 28 May 585 BC, which halts a battle between the Lydians and the Medes. Pythagoras is born on Samos around 570 BC.
Cyrus II overthrows Astyages of Media in 553–550 BC and founds the Persian Empire. He defeats Croesus near the Halys and completes the conquest of Lydia in 546 BC, with Pasargadae his capital.
Confucius is born in 551 BC and dies in 479 BC; a temple to him is founded at Qufu the next year.
Carthage conquers Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica in the 550s BC and takes Gadir around 501 BC.
Cambyses II conquers Egypt in 525 BC; Darius I completes the occupation of the Punjab in 516 BC and makes Aramaic the official language of the western empire.
The state of Wu, with Sun Tzu, defeats Chu at Boju in 506 BC.
The Buddha dies around 483 BC; the First Buddhist Council meets at Rajgaha.
The first part of the Grand Canal of China is dug in 486 BC.
In 480 BC, the year of Salamis, the Greeks of Sicily defeat the Carthaginians at Himera.
The Parthenon is begun in 447 BC and completed in 438 BC. Herodotus finishes his Histories around 449 BC and Aeschylus the Oresteia in 458 BC; Rome publishes the Twelve Tables in 449 BC.
Democritus proposes around 440 BC that matter is made of indivisible particles, atoms. Hippocrates had been born on Kos around 460 BC.
The Jōmon period of Japan ends around 400 BC.
Athens sentences Socrates to death in 399 BC. His pupil Plato founds the Academy in Athens in 387 BC, where mathematics, astronomy and philosophy are taught.
Gauls under Brennus defeat the Romans at the Allia in 387 BC, nine years after Camillus destroyed Veii.
The Second Buddhist Council meets at Vaisali around 383 BC.
Shang Yang begins his reforms of the state of Qin in 356 BC.
Alexander defeats Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BC and ends Persian hegemony. He beats Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BC and dies at Babylon in 323 BC, where his generals divide the conquests.
Ptolemy founds the Museum and Library of Alexandria around 307 BC, with about a hundred scholars. The Pharos is completed there around 285 BC.
Chandragupta Maurya defeats Seleucus I around 304 BC; in the settlement he gives Seleucus 500 war elephants.
Pyrrhus of Epirus invades Italy in 280 BC, the year the Colossus of Rhodes is completed.
Ashoka rules the Mauryan Empire from about 273 to 232 BC. After the Kalinga war he has his edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars across India.
Rome and Carthage go to war over Sicily in 264 BC; the war ends in Carthage’s defeat in 241 BC.
Qin defeats Zhao at Changping in 260 BC. Between 225 and 222 BC Qin conquers Wei, Chu, Yan and Zhao.
An Dương Vương overthrows the Hồng Bàng dynasty in Vietnam in 258–257 BC; Zhao Tuo defeats him in 208 BC and founds the Triệu dynasty of Nanyue.
Li Bing builds the Dujiangyan irrigation system on the Min river in Sichuan in 256 BC.
Two years after crossing the Alps, Hannibal destroys a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BC.
Qin Shi Huang, who has unified China in 221 BC, orders the building of the Great Wall against the northern nomads in 214 BC. He dies in 210 BC and his dynasty falls in 206 BC.
The Romans defeat Carthage in Africa in 202 BC and end the Second Punic War. In China Liu Bang founds the Han dynasty the same year.
The Xiongnu of the steppe defeat the new Han dynasty at Baideng in 200 BC.
Around 200 BC the barangay polities begin to form in the Philippines.
Eratosthenes of Alexandria calculates the circumference of the Earth around 200 BC.
Paper is first made in Han China in the second century BC; Cai Lun’s improved paper follows in AD 105.
Rome defeats Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC, Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC and Perseus at Pydna in 168 BC; the Antigonid kingdom is dissolved.
Ptolemy V is crowned at Memphis in 196 BC, aged fourteen, and the priests issue the decree that is carved on the Rosetta Stone.
Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last Maurya emperor in 185 BC and founds the Shunga dynasty.
The Xiongnu defeat the Yuezhi around 176 BC and the Yuezhi migrate west from Gansu to the Ili valley; the Wusun drive them out of the Ili around 160 BC.
Judas Maccabaeus restores the Temple in Jerusalem on 25 Kislev 164 BC.
In 146 BC, the year it destroys Carthage, Rome razes Corinth and dissolves the Achaean League; Greece is Rome’s.
Emperor Wu begins a reign of 54 years in 141 BC. From the ambush at Mayi in 133 BC the Han make war on the Xiongnu.
Scipio Aemilianus takes Numantia in Spain in 133 BC.
Hipparchus compiles a large star catalogue around 130 BC and calculates the precession of the equinoxes.

Teotihuacan is founded in the Valley of Mexico around 100 BC, and the Pyramid of the Sun is complete by about AD 100. At its height around 450 the city covers some 30 km² and may hold 150,000 people; its great monuments are sacked and burned around 550. The Aztecs, who found it in ruins, give it its name.
Mithridates VI of Pontus has the Romans and Italians of Asia Minor massacred in 88 BC; 80,000 are killed. Rome’s Mithridatic wars end only with his suicide in 63 BC.
In 88 BC Sulla becomes the first Roman general to march on Rome; he does it again in 83 BC and is made dictator in 81 BC.
Spartacus leads the slave revolt of the Third Servile War from 73 BC; Pompey and Crassus end it in 71 BC.
Pompey clears the Mediterranean of pirates in forty days in 67 BC, drives Mithridates out of Asia Minor and takes Jerusalem in 63 BC.
By tradition the Korean kingdom of Silla is founded in 57 BC.
The Parthians destroy the army of Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC.
A Maya numeral for zero is written at Chiapa in 36 BC.
The Han census completed in AD 2 counts 59,594,978 people.
Wang Mang deposes the Han child-emperor in AD 9 and founds the Xin dynasty; the Eastern Han is established in 25.
The Trưng sisters lead the Vietnamese against Han rule in 40–43; the rising is put down.
Boudica of the Iceni rises against Roman rule in Britain in 60.

The Great Fire of Rome in 64 destroys two-thirds of the city and Nero’s persecution of the Christians begins. Tradition holds that Peter, counted the first bishop of Rome, is crucified under Nero between 64 and 68 and buried on the Vatican Hill, where Constantine later builds the basilica over his grave.

events.n: The Year of the Four Emperors
events.t: Four emperors claim Rome in 69 and Vespasian wins. Jerusalem is sacked and the Second Temple destroyed in 70; Masada falls in 73.

events.n: The Han defeat the Northern Xiongnu
events.t: Han armies defeat the Northern Xiongnu at Yiwulu in 73 and in the Altai in 89; the war ends in the Ili valley in 91.
The codex, the bound book of leaves, appears in the Roman Empire around 100. In China Wang Chong describes a chain pump around 80.
A Chola king builds the Grand Anicut dam across the Kaveri in the second century.
Between the first and sixth centuries the Hindu number system develops in the Indian subcontinent, the decimal numerals the world now writes.
The Moche culture develops on the north coast of Peru around AD 100, while Teotihuacan grows to 60,000–80,000 people.
Cai Lun makes modern paper in Han China in 105. Earlier forms of paper had been made there since the second century BC.
Zhang Heng builds a water-powered armillary sphere in 125 and a seismometer in 132 at the Han capital.
Kanishka rules the Kushan Empire across Pakistan and northern India from about 127 to 140. Gandhara’s sculptors carve the Buddha in human form in the second or third century.
Simon bar Kokhba leads the Jews of Judea in revolt against Rome in 132–135, while Hadrian’s Wall is being built in Britain.
Rome builds the Antonine Wall across central Scotland in 142–154, north of Hadrian’s Wall.
Marcus Aurelius fights the Marcomannic Wars on the Danube frontier from 166 to 180, in the years of the Antonine Plague.
The Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 breaks the Han; warlords fight over the court and Cao Cao defeats Yuan Shao at Guandu in 200.
Cao Cao is defeated at the Red Cliffs on the Yangtze in 208. When the Han ends in 220, China divides into the Three Kingdoms.
Caracalla’s Constitutio Antoniniana of 212 grants Roman citizenship to the free people of the empire; the Baths of Caracalla rise in Rome.
Ardashir I defeats the last Parthian king, Artabanus V, at Hormozdgan in 224 and Sasanian rule over Persia begins. In 260 Shapur I captures the Roman emperor Valerian.

events.n: The Crisis of the Third Century
events.t: From 235 to 284 the Roman Empire passes through about fifty years of civil war, invasion and no fewer than twenty emperors, until Diocletian.
Mani preaches his new faith, Manichaeism, at the Sasanian court from 242 to 274.
The Classic period of the Maya begins around AD 250. Tikal and Calakmul are the great rivals; the largest cities hold 50,000 to 120,000 people, and Tikal covers about 20 km².
Sima Yan founds the Jin dynasty in 266 and reunites China in 280 by conquering Eastern Wu.
Diocletian reigns from 284 to 305 and in 293 divides the rule of the empire among four emperors, the Tetrarchy.
The Kofun era of great keyhole-shaped tombs begins in Japan around 300 and lasts until 538.
The Sixteen Kingdoms period begins in northern China in 304, and around 317 the Jin court retreats south of the Yangtze; the Eastern Jin rules from Jiankang.
Butuan Boat One is built in the Philippines around 320.
The Gupta Empire is established in northern India early in the fourth century, and Samudragupta expands it in 335–380.
The stirrup is invented in China no later than 322.
Around 350 the Kingdom of Aksum conquers the Kingdom of Kush on the middle Nile, twenty years after Aksum adopts Christianity.
The Mulavarman inscription of eastern Borneo, around 350, is the earliest in Indonesia.
An earthquake of magnitude at least eight and a tsunami strike the eastern Mediterranean in 365.
In January 378 Siyaj K’ak’, a lord tied to Teotihuacan, conquers Waka, Tikal and Uaxactun and replaces the king of Tikal.
Chandragupta II’s reign of about 380–415 is the golden age of the Gupta Empire of northern India. Skandagupta, the last great Gupta emperor, rules until 467.
The Eastern Jin defeat Fu Jian’s invasion at the Fei river in 383.
Theodosius I dies in 395 and the Roman Empire splits permanently into East and West. He had banned pagan worship and the First Council of Constantinople had reaffirmed the Trinity in 381.
The Chinese monk Faxian leaves for India in 399 to gather Buddhist texts. He travels through India and Sri Lanka and is home by 412.
Mesrop Mashtots introduces the Armenian alphabet in 405; 36 of its 38 letters are his.
Three years after the sack of Rome, Augustine begins The City of God at Hippo in 413.
K’inich Yax K’uk’ Mo’ re-establishes Copán in 426. At Tikal the North Acropolis is built in the fifth century.
The Ilopango volcano in El Salvador erupts around 430 and devastates the nearby Maya cities.
The Vandals conquer Carthage in 439 and sack Rome in 455.
The Hopewell tradition of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys comes to an end in the fifth century.

Romans and Visigoths defeat Attila’s Huns on the Catalaunian Plains in 451. Attila destroys Aquileia the next year, is turned from Rome by Pope Leo I and dies in 453; his empire falls apart after Nedao in 454.
The fourth ecumenical council meets at Chalcedon in 451, the year of the Catalaunian Plains. Ephesus had upheld the title Theotokos for Mary in 431.
Theodoric the Ostrogoth ousts Odoacer and becomes king of Italy in 493.
The Shaolin Monastery is founded on Mount Song in 477 or 495, in the age of the Northern and Southern dynasties.

From about AD 500 the Wari state, ruled from Huari near Ayacucho, spreads over much of the Peruvian highlands and coast. Its records are kept on knotted khipu, perhaps first used here, and its sites lie along the later Inca roads; drought weakens it from about 800 and Huari is largely empty by 1000.
The Romans obtain silkworm eggs around 522 and begin to raise silk in the Eastern Empire.
Dionysius Exiguus devises the Anno Domini system of counting years at Rome in 525.
Benedict of Nursia founds the monastery of Monte Cassino in 529. Boethius had written The Consolation of Philosophy in prison around 524.
In the Nika riots at Constantinople in 532 the cathedral is destroyed and up to 30,000 people are killed.
Nobatia converts to Christianity in 545, and Alodia and Makuria in 569.
Maya nobles practise dental modification, and some lords wear jade set into their teeth.
Teotihuacan, at its height from about AD 150 to 450, declines in the sixth century. Its sacking is recorded but not dated.
Bumin Khagan founds the first Turkic Khaganate on the Mongolian steppe in 551. It is destroyed by the Tang in 629–630.
Muhammad is born at Mecca around 570.
The builders Kongō Gumi are founded at Osaka in 578.
Gregory the Great becomes pope in 590 and sends Augustine’s monks to England in 595.
The temple of Hōryū-ji at Ikaruga is believed completed in 607.

The Sasanians sack Jerusalem in 615 and take the True Cross; Khosrow II invades Egypt in 616. Heraclius defeats the Persians in 627, ending the Roman–Persian wars, five years before the Muslim conquests begin.
K’inich Janaab’ Pakal becomes king of the Maya city of Palenque in 615.
The Muslim victory at al-Qadisiyyah in 636 opens Persia; Yazdegerd III is murdered at Merv in 651 and Sasanian rule ends. Palestine falls in 638 and Egypt in 639.
The Arab armies are defeated in Nubia at Dongola in 642 and again in 652, and the baqt treaty follows.
China issues its first paper money in 650, under the Tang.
Ali is assassinated in 661 and Muawiyah I begins the Umayyad Caliphate at Damascus. Husayn is killed at Karbala in 680.
Tang and Silla defeat Baekje and its Yamato allies at Baekgang in 663; Goguryeo falls in 668 and Unified Silla rules the peninsula.
Uqba ibn Nafi enters Ifriqiya in 670; the Arabs take Carthage from the Byzantines in 698.
The pilgrim I-tsing visits Srivijaya in 671 on his way to Nalanda. From 683 Srivijaya holds the Straits of Malacca and Sunda, and in 686 it invades Java.
The first Arab siege of Constantinople begins in 674; in 677 Greek fire destroys most of the Arab fleet.
The Bulgars beat the Byzantines at Ongal in 680, and in 681 Byzantium recognises Bulgaria as independent.
Wu Zetian seizes power as Empress of China in 690 and makes Buddhism the state religion in 691.
Japan enacts the Taihō legal code in 701 and moves its capital to Heijō-kyō, Nara, in 710. The Nara period begins.
Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses the strait at Gibraltar in 711 and al-Andalus is created; the Treaty of Tudmir follows in 713. In the same year, 711, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim invades Sindh.

events.n: The wars of the Maya cities
events.t: The Maya kingdoms of the Classic age fight among themselves: Toniná conquers Palenque in 711, and Quiriguá declares its independence from Copán in 738.
The Umayyad siege of Constantinople in 717–718 fails and the Arab advance into Europe from the east is halted. At Akroinon in 740 the Byzantines win their first large victory over the Arabs.
Leo III removes the image of Christ above the Chalke Gate in 726 and Iconoclasm begins. Empress Irene’s Seventh Ecumenical Council restores the icons in 787.
Bede completes the Ecclesiastical History of the English People in 731, a year before Tours.
A census of 742 counts 362,921 families and 1,960,188 people in the Chang’an district, the capital of Tang China under Xuanzong, whose reign of 712–756 is a high point for China.
The last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, is overthrown and executed in 750, and the Abbasid Caliphate begins under al-Saffah. Al-Mansur succeeds him in 754; the Abbasids rule from Iraq.
In the middle of the eighth century papermaking passes from China to the Arabs, in the years of the battle of Talas near Samarkand. The Han Chinese had made paper since the second century BC.
The An Shi rebellion of 755–763 devastates Tang China, four years after the defeat at Talas.
Construction of Borobudur begins in Java around 760; the great Buddhist monument is completed under Samaratungga in 825.
Charlemagne campaigns against the Saxons for more than thirty years, from 772 to 804.
Emperor Kanmu moves the capital to Heian-kyō, today’s Kyoto, in 794.
In the ninth century the political order of the central Maya lowlands collapses. The Post-Classic begins, and Chichén Itzá in the Yucatán becomes a regional capital.
Jayavarman II founds the Khmer empire in 802 and the Angkorian dynasty begins.
The Giant Buddha carved in the rock at Leshan is completed in 803 after 90 years of work.
Al-Khwarizmi writes his treatise on algebra at Baghdad around 820, and al-Ma’mun founds the House of Wisdom there in 830.
The Treaty of Verdun divides the Carolingian Empire into three in 843, three years after the death of Louis the Pious.
Chinese alchemists of the Tang invent gunpowder in the ninth century. Its first use in battle is recorded at Langshan Jiang in 919.
In the ninth century the Igbo of southern Nigeria cast elaborate bronzes, some of them buried with the dead at Igbo-Ukwu.
Al-Qarawiyyin is founded as a madrasa at Fez in 859.
The Diamond Sutra, printed from woodblocks in 868, is the earliest known printed book.
Enslaved East Africans rise against the Abbasids in southern Iraq in the Zanj rebellion of 869–883. In China the Huang Chao rebellion against the Tang follows in 875–884.
Alfred the Great defeats Guthrum’s Danes at Ethandun in 878.
The Fatimid Caliphate rises among the Kutama of North Africa around 909. Cairo is founded beside Fustat in 969; it becomes the Fatimid capital in 972, and al-Azhar is established around 980.
Goryeo unifies the Later Three Kingdoms of Korea in 936.
Vietnamese forces win at the Bạch Đằng river in 938 and end the long Chinese domination of Vietnam.
The Nri kingdom of the Igbo begins in south-eastern Nigeria around 948.
The Tuʻi Tonga dynasty of Tonga is formed around 950. In the twelfth century its kings extend their reach across the islands of the western Pacific.
Otto I defeats the Hungarians at the Lechfeld in 955; seven years later he is crowned emperor.
The prince of Kiev defeats the Khazar kingdom on the lower Volga in 965.
The Ghaznavids establish the first Turkic sultanate around 975 and conquer the Samanids in 999. The Seljuks convert to Islam in 960.
Queen Gudit rises against the Aksumite dynasty of Abyssinia around 980.
In 987 Ah Mekat Tutul Xiu unites Uxmal, Mayapan and Chichén Itzá in the Yucatán, which becomes a regional capital of the Post-Classic Maya.
The Tiwanaku state by Lake Titicaca collapses in the first half of the eleventh century. In Mexico the Toltec and Mixtec civilisations flourish.
Mahmud of Ghazni begins his raids into northern India in 1001.
Held under house arrest in Cairo from 1011 to 1021, Ibn al-Haytham writes his Book of Optics. Cairo’s Dar al-Hikma had been founded in 1004.
Basil II defeats Samuil of Bulgaria at Kleidion in 1014 and by 1018 has conquered the First Bulgarian Empire. In Ireland Brian Boru is killed winning at Clontarf in 1014.
Rajendra Chola I’s navy strikes across the Bay of Bengal in 1025 and makes Srivijaya a vassal. He moves his capital to Gangaikonda Cholapuram.
An earthquake and tsunami strike the Jordan valley and the coast of Palestine in 1033 and kill tens of thousands.
In the years 1041–1048 Bi Sheng makes ceramic movable type in Song China, four centuries before Gutenberg. The Song military manual Wujing Zongyao of 1044 gives formulas for gunpowder.
The Mississippian culture flourishes in the eleventh century. Its great town at Cahokia, on the Mississippi below the Missouri, grows in the thirteenth century to a population that rivals London’s.
Chinese astronomers record a new star in 1054, the year of the Great Schism. Its remnant is the Crab Nebula.
The Seljuk Turks take Baghdad in 1055, beat the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071 and take Jerusalem from the Fatimids in 1074. Pope Urban II calls the First Crusade in 1095.
Anawrahta of Pagan defeats Thaton in 1057 and unifies Myanmar.
Arab tribes of the Banu Hilal invade Ifriqiya and destroy Kairouan in 1057.
The Almoravids sack Koumbi Saleh, capital of the Ghana Empire, in 1076. Ten years later they cross to Spain and defeat Castile at az-Zallaqah, a year after Alfonso VI took Toledo.
Emperor Henry IV humbles himself before Pope Gregory VII at Canossa in 1077.
The University of Bologna is established in 1088.
Shen Kuo’s Dream Pool Essays of 1088 first describe the magnetic needle compass. Su Song’s astronomical clock tower at Kaifeng is finished in 1094.
The Ife Empire of the Yoruba is established in West Africa in the twelfth century; it collapses around 1420.
Mayapan rises to dominance in the Yucatán in the twelfth century after the decline of Chichén Itzá, whose Great Ballcourt is the largest in Mesoamerica; it is abandoned around 1448.
Venice founds its Arsenal in 1104, the shipyard that in time employs about 16,000 workers.
Suryavarman II is crowned at Angkor in 1113, and under him Angkor Wat is built.
The Knights Templar are founded at Jerusalem in 1119; the Teutonic Knights follow at Acre in 1198.
The Georgians, 45,000 strong with their allies, defeat a Seljuk-led coalition at Didgori in 1121. Tbilisi becomes the Georgian capital in 1122, ending 400 years of Arab rule.

events.fig: 52,000 men in the Song navy by 1183
events.t: The Jurchen Jin declare war on the Song in 1125 and take northern China in 1127. The Southern Song found China’s first permanent standing navy in 1132; by 1183 it has 52,000 men, and the treaty of 1141 sets the border on the Huai.
A fifty-year drought settles on the American Southwest from 1130, and the Chaco Canyon culture of the Ancestral Puebloans collapses between 1140 and 1150.
Abbot Suger begins rebuilding the abbey church of Saint-Denis north of Paris in 1136, and the Gothic style begins.

events.n: The Almohads and the siege of Lisbon
events.t: The Almohads take North Africa from the Almoravids in 1147; the same year crusaders and Portuguese take Lisbon after a four-month siege.
Tula, the city of the Toltecs, burns in the twelfth century and the Toltec empire ends.
Al-Idrisi publishes his Geography in 1154, the year Henry II is crowned in England.
Saladin ends the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt in 1171 and founds the Ayyubid dynasty. Sixteen years later he destroys the crusader army at Hattin.
The Minamoto and the Taira fight the Genpei War in Japan from 1180 to 1185. Hōnen had founded the Pure Land sect in 1175.
The first record of windmills in Europe dates from 1185.
Saladin destroys the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Horns of Hattin on 4 July 1187 and takes Jerusalem. The Third Crusade follows; Barbarossa drowns in the Salef in 1190.
Muhammad of Ghor establishes the first Muslim empire in northern India in 1192; the monastery-university of Nalanda is destroyed in 1193.
Fibonacci introduces the Liber Abaci in 1202.
The Delhi Sultanate is established in northern India in 1206 under the Mamluk dynasty, the year Genghis Khan is proclaimed.

events.n: The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
events.t: The Christian kingdoms defeat the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Portugal completes its reconquest with the Algarve in 1249.
The kingdom of Mapungubwe is established on the Limpopo around 1220. Later in the century the Kingdom of Zimbabwe is founded, and in Ethiopia the Solomonic dynasty replaces the Zagwe in 1270.
The Mongols destroy Merv, Herat, Bamyan and Nishapur in 1221, the cities of the Khwarazmian Empire.
A Mongol army defeats the Russian princes on the Kalka river in 1223, fourteen years before the great invasion.
The Mandinka kingdoms unite to form the Mali Empire in 1235.

events.n: The Mongol invasion of Rus and Europe
events.t: The Mongols conquer Kievan Rus in 1237–1240. In 1241 they defeat the Poles at Legnica and the Hungarians at Mohi.
Russians defeat a Swedish army on the Neva in 1240 and the Teutonic Knights on the ice of Lake Peipus in 1242.
Cliff Palace and the other Ancestral Pueblo towns of Mesa Verde reach their height around 1250.
The Mongols take and destroy Baghdad in 1258 and end the Abbasid Caliphate.
The Mamluks of Egypt inflict the first major defeat on the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260. The Mamluks take Antioch in 1268 and Acre, the last crusader city, in 1291.
Thomas Aquinas begins the Summa Theologiae in 1265. In 1277 the bishop of Paris condemns propositions drawn from Aristotle.

events.n: Marco Polo’s journey to Kublai Khan
events.t: Niccolò, Maffeo and the young Marco Polo leave Venice in 1271, sail to Acre and Hormuz and ride the Silk Road to Kublai Khan’s summer palace at Shangdu, probably in 1275. Marco serves the Khan for seventeen years. They sail home in 1291 escorting the princess Kököchin; only 18 of about 600 passengers survive, and the Polos reach Venice in 1295, where Marco later dictates his book to Rustichello da Pisa in a Genoese prison.
Kublai Khan’s fleets invade Japan in 1274 and 1281 and are both times repelled.
The Song dynasty ends with defeat by the Mongols at sea off Yamen in 1279, and all China is under Yuan rule.
A Mongol invasion of Java is repelled in 1293 and Majapahit is founded in eastern Java the same year.
Wang Zhen invents wooden movable type in China in 1298.
Osman I establishes the Ottoman state in north-western Anatolia in 1299.
The papal seat moves from Rome to Avignon in 1309 and stays until 1377. The return is followed in 1378 by the Western Schism, with two and then three rival popes until 1417.
Years of rain and failed harvests from 1315 to 1317 bring the Great Famine to northern Europe. Millions die, a generation before the Black Death.
Dante completes the Divine Comedy in 1321, the poem of a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise.

events.fig: 80 camels with 300 pounds of gold each
events.t: In the seventeenth year of his reign Musa I of Mali goes on pilgrimage to Mecca with about 60,000 men and 80 camels each carrying 300 pounds of gold. He floods the Cairo market with so much gold that its value had not recovered twelve years later; on the way home he brings the poet and architect al-Sahili, who builds him a mosque at Timbuktu.
src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mūsā I of Mali

events.t: Ibn Battuta leaves Tangier for Mecca on 14 June 1325 and travels for almost thirty years: Cairo, Baghdad, the Swahili coast, the Golden Horde and Constantinople, Delhi, where he serves Muhammad bin Tughluq as a judge, the Maldives and Quanzhou. He crosses the Sahara to Mali and Timbuktu in 1352 and dictates the Rihla to Ibn Juzayy around 1355.
The Mexica found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325. Acamapichtli is accepted as its first tlatoani in 1366; within a century the island town is the capital of the Aztec Empire.
Harihara I founds the Vijayanagara Empire in South India in 1336. It rules the south for more than two centuries, until the Deccan sultanates defeat it at Talikota in 1565.
Ramathibodi I establishes the kingdom of Ayutthaya in Siam in 1350; Fa Ngum founds Lan Xang in Laos three years later.
The first Diet of the Hansa meets at Lübeck in 1356 and formalises the Hanseatic League, the merchant league of the Baltic and North Sea towns.
The Red Turban rebellions, begun along the Huai in 1351, end Mongol Yuan rule. The Yuan dynasty ends and the Ming dynasty begins in 1368, with its first capital at Nanjing.
English peasants rise in 1381, the year Wycliffe is dismissed from Oxford. It is the century of revolts after the plague: the Ciompi in Florence (1378–82) and the Red Turbans in China.
Two years after Kulikovo, Khan Tokhtamysh of the Golden Horde takes Moscow in 1382. The Horde’s overlordship of the Russian principalities lasts another century.

The Ottomans and the Serbs meet at Kosovo Polje in 1389; Prince Lazar and Sultan Murad I are both killed. At Nicopolis on the Danube in 1396 the Ottomans defeat a large crusader army, and the Second Bulgarian Empire ends with Vidin the same year.
Taejo founds the Joseon dynasty in Korea in 1392, the same year Japan’s two rival courts are reunited.
Norway, Sweden and Denmark are united under one crown at Kalmar in 1397.
Timur defeats the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402 and captures Sultan Bayezid I. Ten years of civil war among Bayezid’s sons follow, the Ottoman Interregnum of 1403–1413.
Parameswara, a prince who fled Palembang, founds Malacca on the strait in 1402. It becomes the great port between the Indian Ocean and the China Sea until Albuquerque takes it in 1511.
Poland and Lithuania defeat the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410, the beginning of the order’s downfall.
Henry the Navigator takes Ceuta in 1415, the first Portuguese foothold in Africa and the start of a century of voyages down the African coast.
The Council of Constance burns the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus in 1415. The Hussite Wars follow in Bohemia from 1419 and end at Lipany in 1434.
The Yongle Emperor moves the Ming capital to Beijing, and the Forbidden City is completed in 1420.
Itzcoatl begins his reign at Tenochtitlan in 1427 and is counted the first Aztec emperor; Moctezuma I follows in 1440. The city on the lake becomes the head of an empire of tribute.
Joan of Arc ends the English siege of Orléans in 1429. She is tried at Rouen and burned there on 30 May 1431, aged nineteen.
The Inca hold the coca leaf sacred and use it in moderation against hunger and pain; the chasqui runners who carry messages on the roads chew it for strength.

Pachacuti begins the expansion of the Inca state from Cusco in 1438. Topa Inca conquers the Chimú kingdom from 1463 and pushes north into Ecuador; in the south the empire reaches the Maule in Chile. By about 1527 Tawantinsuyu covers some 2,000,000 km², with about 12 million people, linked by roads, runners and knotted quipu records; Pizarro takes Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532.
Oba Ewuare comes to power in Benin around 1440 and builds up the kingdom and its city in West Africa.
In 1441 a Portuguese ship brings captives from West Africa directly to Portugal. It is the start of the Portuguese seaborne trade in enslaved Africans.
King Sejong of Joseon publishes hangul in 1443, an alphabet made for Korean. King Taejong’s court had first used movable type in 1403.
The Oirat leader Esen captures the Zhengtong Emperor at Tumu Fortress in 1449.

events.fig: more than 140 children and about 200 llamas
events.t: On a bluff near Huanchaco, on the Chimú coast of Peru, more than 140 children aged about 5 to 14 and some 200 young llamas are sacrificed around 1450. The excavators, Gabriel Prieto and John Verano, think it was an offering against El Niño rains and floods; their 2019 paper in PLOS ONE counts 137 children.
src: National Geographic, Exclusive: Ancient mass child sacrifice may be world’s largest
PBS NOVA, What prompted the mass sacrifice of hundreds of children and llamas in ancient Peru?

events.t: The Inca build Machu Picchu on a ridge above the Urubamba in the 1450s, in the years of Pachacuti’s expansion.

events.fig: more than 150 copies, about 20 complete today
events.t: Johann Gutenberg’s shop at Mainz prints a large-format Latin Bible between 1454 and 1456, the first great book of European printing. More than 150 copies are made; about 20 survive complete. Gutenberg may have begun working on the technique as early as the 1430s.
src: Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas, The Gutenberg Bible

events.t: Civil war breaks out in 1467 and opens the Sengoku period, more than a century of warring states in Japan.
Muscovy annexes the merchant republic of Novgorod in 1478. Two years later the stand on the Ugra ends the Horde’s overlordship.
Bartolomeu Dias sails round the southern tip of Africa in 1488 and proves the sea route east. Six years earlier Diogo Cão had entered the mouth of the Congo.

events.n: The expulsion of the Jews from Spain
events.t: The Alhambra Decree of 1492 orders the Jews of Spain to convert or leave. Between 40,000 and 200,000 leave, the year Granada falls and Columbus sails.

events.n: Guru Nanak and the Sikh faith
events.t: Guru Nanak, born in the Punjab in 1469, begins to preach around 1500. His teaching is the beginning of Sikhism.
The Safavid dynasty reunifies Iran in 1501 and rules until 1736. Ottomans and Safavids fight at Chaldiran in 1514, and the Ottomans take Baghdad from them in 1534.
Afonso I wins the battle of Mbanza Kongo in 1506 and makes Catholicism the state religion of the kingdom of Kongo.
Afonso de Albuquerque takes Hormuz and Muscat in 1507, Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511. The victory at Diu in 1509 begins Portuguese dominance of the spice trade.
The first recorded smallpox epidemic in the New World devastates the Taíno of Hispaniola in 1507. Five years earlier the first enslaved Africans had been reported in the Americas.
Michelangelo paints the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel from 1508 to 1512, a few years after his David for Florence and his Pietà for Rome.
Machiavelli writes The Prince in 1513, the year Balboa crosses the isthmus of Panama and sees the Pacific.
Selim I defeats the Mamluks in 1516–1517 and gains Egypt, Arabia and the Levant. Under Suleiman from 1520 the empire reaches its zenith: Belgrade in 1521, Rhodes in 1522, Mohács in 1526.
Peasants rise across the Holy Roman Empire in 1524–1525, seven years after Luther’s theses.

On 21 April 1526 Babur, with about 12,000 men, matchlocks and cannon, defeats Ibrahim Lodi’s 50,000 or more and 1,000 war elephants at Panipat. Ibrahim and about 20,000 of his men are killed; the guns panic the elephants, and the victory founds the Mughal Empire.
Troops of Charles V sack Rome in 1527, two years after his armies captured Francis I of France at Pavia.
The Church of England breaks from Rome in 1531–1532 under Henry VIII; Anne Boleyn is beheaded in 1536.

events.n: São Vicente, the first Portuguese town in Brazil
events.t: São Vicente, founded in 1532, is the first permanent Portuguese settlement in the Americas. Buenos Aires is founded by Pedro de Mendoza in 1536 and Cartier claims Canada for France in 1534.
Portuguese traders reach Japan in 1543 and open the Nanban trade. Firearms are used on a Japanese battlefield at Uedahara in 1548.
The Shaanxi earthquake of 1556 is the deadliest known in the Ming era. The same year Akbar wins the second battle of Panipat.
Habsburg Spain declares bankruptcy in 1557, the first of four state bankruptcies under Philip II (1557, 1560, 1575, 1596).
The Deccan sultanates defeat the Vijayanagara Empire at Talikota in 1565.
Huguenots are massacred in Paris on St Bartholomew’s Day 1572. The French Wars of Religion end only with the Edict of Nantes in 1598.
King Sebastian of Portugal is killed fighting in Morocco in 1578. In 1580 Spain and Portugal are united under Philip II, for sixty years.
The Gregorian calendar is introduced in 1582 and ten days are skipped to bring the year back into line with the sun.
After Oda Nobunaga’s death at Honnō-ji in 1582, Toyotomi Hideyoshi completes the unification of Japan with the siege of Odawara in 1590.

events.fig: 138 ships and over 25,000 men; about 67 returned
events.t: Philip II’s Armada leaves Lisbon on 30 May 1588 with 138 ships and over 25,000 seamen and soldiers to carry an army from Flanders to England. It is sighted off the Lizard on 29 July and fought up the Channel; eight English fireships break its anchorage off Calais on the night of 7 August and the fleet is beaten at Gravelines on 8 August. Driven north round Scotland and Ireland, about 19 ships are wrecked; only around 67 return to Spain and up to 11,000 men may have died.
src: Royal Museums Greenwich, History of the Spanish Armada
Wikipedia, List of ships of the Spanish Armada

events.t: A Moroccan army defeats the Songhai Empire at Tondibi in 1591; the old Mali Empire is defeated at Jenné in 1599.
Hideyoshi’s armies invade Korea twice between 1592 and 1598. Korea, with Ming help, repels both invasions; the war ends with Hideyoshi’s death in 1598.

events.n: The first Dutch voyage to the Indies
events.t: The first Dutch expedition sails for the East Indies in 1595 with 249 men and 64 cannon. Seven years later the Dutch East India Company is founded.
Romeo and Juliet is published in 1597. Shakespeare, baptised in 1564, is the same age as Galileo, born at Pisa that February.
Giordano Bruno is burned for heresy in Rome in 1600.

events.n: The East India Company is chartered
events.t: On 31 December 1600 Elizabeth I grants a royal charter to the Earl of Cumberland and 218 others trading to the East Indies. James Lancaster sails on the first voyage in the Red Dragon in 1601; the Company opens trading posts at Surat and Madras and moves to Calcutta after 1690.
Tokugawa Ieyasu wins the battle of Sekigahara in 1600, two years after Hideyoshi’s death. In 1603 he becomes shogun and the Edo period begins; it lasts until 1868.

events.n: The Time of Troubles and the Romanovs
events.fig: about a third of the population dead in the famine
events.t: Famine in 1601–1603 kills about a third of Russia’s people. A Polish–Lithuanian army beats the Russians and Swedes at Klushino in 1610 and takes Moscow; in 1613 the Time of Troubles ends with the election of the first Romanov tsar, whose dynasty rules until 1917.

events.n: Matteo Ricci’s map of the world
events.t: The Jesuit Matteo Ricci makes a map of the world in China in 1602; it is used across East Asia.
Willem Janszoon makes the first recorded European landing on the Australian mainland in 1606.
The Dutch hold Jayakarta against a siege in 1619 and build Batavia on its site, the capital of the VOC’s Asian empire. Sultan Agung of Mataram fails to take it in 1628–1629.
The first Africans are brought to Virginia in 1619, twelve years after Jamestown. In 1622 Algonquian warriors kill 347 settlers outside Jamestown.
Shah Jahan begins the Taj Mahal at Agra in 1632. His son Aurangzeb deposes him in 1658.
After the Shimabara rebellion of Christians and peasants in 1637, Japan becomes a locked country under sakoku between 1633 and 1639.
Blaise Pascal builds a mechanical calculator in 1642 and Evangelista Torricelli the mercury barometer in 1643. Huygens makes the first working pendulum clock in 1657.
Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s Cossacks rise against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1648, the year of the Peace of Westphalia.
The Royal Society is founded in London in 1660. Robert Hooke sees cells through a microscope in 1665 and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discovers bacteria in 1676.
Portugal defeats the kingdom of Kongo at Mbwila in Angola in 1665.
The Great Fire of London burns the old city in 1666.
Shivaji crowns himself Chhatrapati in 1674 and founds the Maratha Empire against the Mughals. He had visited Aurangzeb at Agra in 1666.
The Pueblo peoples rise in 1680 and drive the Spanish out of New Mexico until 1692.
Robert de La Salle claims the lands of the Mississippi for France in 1682. New Orleans is founded in 1718.
The Qing conquer the Kingdom of Tungning in 1683 and annex Taiwan, the year the Ottomans fail before Vienna.
The Bank of England is established in 1694, in the reign of William and Mary after the Glorious Revolution.

Peter’s first siege of Azov in 1695 fails. In 1696 he returns with about 75,000 men and a fleet built at Voronezh of two ships of the line, four fireships and 23 galleys; the Ottoman garrison of about 7,000 surrenders on 19 July. The Boyar Duma’s decree of 20 October 1696 is counted the birth of the Russian navy, and Taganrog becomes its first base.

The Grand Embassy sets out on 9 March 1697 with the tsar travelling incognito as Peter Mikhailov. He is refused a look at the fortifications of Riga, spends two months with an artillery engineer at Königsberg, reaches Zaandam on 18 August 1697 and works in the Amsterdam yards, then lives at Deptford from January to April 1698. News of the Streltsy rising cuts short his stay in Vienna and he is back in Moscow in early September 1698.
src: Wikipedia, Grand Embassy of Peter the Great

events.t: Martín de Ursúa takes the Itza capital Nojpetén in 1697, and independent Maya rule ends, 176 years after the fall of Tenochtitlan.
The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 cedes most of Hungary to the Habsburgs. The Ottoman retreat from central Europe has begun.
The battle of Feyiase in 1701 marks the rise of the Asante Empire in the forest of the Gold Coast.
Aurangzeb dies in 1707 and the Mughal Empire begins to break apart; in the same year the Act of Union joins the parliaments of Scotland and England.
Thomas Newcomen’s steam engine of 1712 pumps water from mines, thirteen years after Thomas Savery showed a steam pump to the Royal Society. Cristofori had built the first piano in Florence in 1709.
Shares in the South Sea Company soar and collapse in London in 1720, the year the Great Plague of Marseille begins.

In 1730 Mikhail Lomonosov, a nineteen-year-old from the village of Mishaninskaya near Kholmogory on the White Sea, walks all the way to Moscow to study. He enters the Slavic Greek Latin Academy by claiming to be a nobleman’s son; in 1755 he helps Count Shuvalov found Moscow University.
Vitus Bering, sailing for Russia from Kamchatka, reaches Alaska in 1741.

events.fig: more than 3,500 pages in the English translation
events.t: Giacomo Casanova, born in Venice in 1725, takes his degree at Padua and serves in Rome and Corfu. He is in Paris in 1750, escapes the Piombi prison of Venice and is back in Paris in January 1757, visits Voltaire in Switzerland in 1760 and London in 1763, Berlin and Catherine’s St Petersburg in the mid-1760s, and is expelled from Warsaw after a duel in 1766. From 1785 he is librarian at Dux in Bohemia, where he writes his Histoire de ma vie and dies in 1798.
Muhammad ibn Saud founds the first Saudi state in Arabia in 1744. In 1747 Ahmad Shah Durrani founds the Durrani Empire in Afghanistan.
Under the Qianlong Emperor the Qing destroy the Dzungar Khanate; the genocide of 1755 depopulates northern Xinjiang.
The Maratha Empire is defeated at Panipat in 1761, the third great battle on the same field.
Catherine the Great’s reign begins in 1762. Her wars with the Ottomans win Russia the Black Sea shore, and Poland is partitioned from 1772.
The Burmese invade Siam in 1765–1767 and destroy Ayutthaya, the capital since 1350.

After Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764 the East India Company takes the diwani of Bengal and Bihar in 1765; the Regulating Act of 1773 makes Warren Hastings the first Governor-General. At its height the Company accounts for about half of world trade and its three presidency armies number about 260,000 men. Company rule covers about 1,940,000 km² in 1858, when after the rebellion of 1857 the Government of India Act of 2 August hands India to the Crown.
Spain founds the first of 21 missions in California in 1769.

events.fig: about a third of the population
events.t: Famine kills about a third of the people of Bengal in 1770, five years after the East India Company takes the province’s revenues.
Yemelyan Pugachev’s rebellion against Catherine begins in 1773, two years after the plague riot in Moscow.

Signed on 21 July 1774, the treaty ends the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–74. Russia gains Azov, Kerch and Yenikale, Kinburn on the Dnieper estuary, free passage of the Bosporus and Dardanelles and a voice for the Orthodox Christians of the Ottoman lands; the Crimean Khanate is made independent of the sultan.
src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca

events.t: Cook leaves Plymouth on 12 July 1776, sights Hawaii on 18 January 1778, reaches Nootka Sound in March and passes the Bering Strait in August 1778 before the ice turns him back. He is killed at Kealakekua Bay on 14 February 1779; the ships reach the Nore in October 1780.
src: Wikipedia, Third voyage of James Cook

events.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations in 1776, the year of the American Declaration of Independence and of Watt’s engine.
William Herschel announces the planet Uranus in 1781. Jan Ingenhousz had described photosynthesis in 1779.

Catherine’s manifesto of 19 April 1783, pressed by Potemkin, annexes the Crimean Khanate. The Black Sea Fleet is counted founded on 13 May 1783 with its base at Sevastopol; the Ottomans recognise the loss in a treaty signed on 28 December 1783 (8 January 1784).

Goethe slips away from Karlsbad on 3 September 1786 and crosses the Brenner to Verona, Vicenza and Venice. He reaches Rome on 29 October, sits for Tischbein, sees Naples, Vesuvius, Pompeii and Paestum and tours Sicily in 1787, then stays another year in Rome before going home to Weimar in June 1788.
src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe: Italian journey (1786–88)

events.t: Edward Jenner gives the first smallpox vaccination in 1796. Smallpox was then killing about 400,000 people a year.

Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland sail from A Coruña on 5 June 1799, land at Cumaná in July and travel up the Orinoco and the Casiquiare in 1800. They cross Cuba and the Andes to Quito, reach about 5,878 m on Chimborazo on 23 June 1802, go on to Lima and Mexico, meet Jefferson in Washington and land at Bordeaux in August 1804.
Hanaoka Seishū in Japan gives the first modern general anaesthetic in 1804. In the West anaesthesia is first used in surgery in 1842, and chloroform follows in 1847.
The first steam locomotive runs in 1804, twenty-one years before the Stockton and Darlington Railway. Morphine is isolated the same year.
The Fulani jihad is fought in what is now northern Nigeria from 1804 to 1810, while the Barbary Wars bring American warships to North Africa.
Māori iwi armed with muskets fight one another across New Zealand from 1807 to 1837. In Tasmania the Black War of 1828–1832 nearly destroys the Aboriginal people.
The Portuguese court moves to Rio de Janeiro in 1808. Pedro I declares Brazil independent on 7 September 1822.
For more than six years Wellington’s Anglo-Portuguese army and Spanish guerrillas fight the French in Spain: 60 major battles and 30 sieges, until Vitoria on 21 June 1813 breaks French power there.
Napoleon defeats the Austrians under Archduke Charles at Wagram on 5–6 July 1809; the Treaty of Schönbrunn follows in October.
The Grito de Dolores of 1810 begins the Mexican War of Independence; Mexico is independent in 1821, the year Central America breaks from Spain.

events.fig: about 450,000 cross the Niemen; about 27,000 fit at the Berezina
events.t: About 450,000 men of the Grande Armée cross the Niemen on 24 June 1812. Smolensk is fought on 16–18 August and Borodino on 7 September, the bloodiest day of the wars, with at least 70,000 casualties; Napoleon enters an evacuated, burning Moscow on 14 September. The retreat begins in October; at the Berezina in November only about 27,000 fit soldiers remain, and the last invaders leave Russia on 14 December.
Mount Tambora on Sumbawa erupts in 1815 and kills at least 71,000 people.
Shaka takes power over the Zulu in 1816; by 1828 the Zulu Kingdom is the largest in southern Africa. The British annex it after the war of 1879.
The British East India Company establishes Singapore in 1819.
Liberia is founded in 1820 for freed American slaves.
Nicéphore Niépce makes his first heliographs in 1822 and takes the first photograph in 1827.
France invades Algeria and occupies it in 1830–1831.
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is established in 1830. In Persia the Báb announces his revelation in 1844.

HMS Beagle leaves Plymouth on 27 December 1831 with the young Charles Darwin. She surveys Brazil, the Plate, Tierra del Fuego and the Falklands, rounds to Valparaíso, reaches the Galápagos on 15 September 1835 and crosses the Pacific to Tahiti, New Zealand and Sydney; the voyage ends on 2 October 1836, almost five years after it began.
src: Wikipedia, Second voyage of HMS Beagle

events.t: Commodore Perry’s gunships threaten Edo in 1853–1854 and the policy of sakoku formally ends. Fifteen years later the shogunate falls.
The Bessemer process of 1855 makes mass-produced steel possible; the world’s first oil refinery opens in Romania in 1856.
Maxwell publishes his equations in 1861, Mendel his laws of inheritance in 1865 and Mendeleev the periodic table in 1869.

Gettysburg, fought on 1–3 July 1863, is the turning point of the war: more than 50,000 casualties, about 28,000 of them Confederate. Vicksburg falls the same month and the Union holds the Mississippi; the Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863 had declared free more than 3.5 million of the 4 million enslaved.

events.n: Diamonds and gold in South Africa
events.t: Diamonds are found at Kimberley in 1867 and gold in the Transvaal in 1886.

Napoleon III surrenders at Sedan on 2 September 1870 and is taken prisoner with about 104,000 soldiers. Paris is besieged from September and capitulates on 28 January 1871; by the Treaty of Frankfurt France cedes Alsace-Lorraine and pays 5 billion francs.
The Anglo-Zulu War of 1879 ends in British victory and the annexation of the Zulu Kingdom. In the Andes Chile fights Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific from 1879 to 1883.
Muhammad Ahmad proclaims himself the Mahdi in the Sudan in 1881 and declares war on Egypt, which Britain occupies in 1882. The Mahdist state is crushed at Omdurman in 1898.
Karl Benz builds the first petrol motor car in 1886 and sells the first commercial automobile.
Guglielmo Marconi sends his first radio signals in 1895; in the 1920s radio becomes the entertainment of the world.
Cuba rises against Spain in 1895; the Spanish–American War of 1898 ends Spanish rule in Cuba. In the Philippines the revolution of 1896–1898 ends in a Filipino victory.
Wilhelm Röntgen identifies X-rays in 1895 and Henri Becquerel discovers radioactivity in 1896.
Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa in 1896, twelve years after the Berlin Conference divided Africa among the European powers.
The Boxer Rebellion in northern China is suppressed by the Eight-Nation Alliance in 1900–1901.

Russia’s Baltic squadron under Rozhestvensky sails for about seven months to relieve Port Arthur and arrives too late. In May 1905 the Japanese fleet destroys it in the Tsushima strait, the most crushing defeat in the history of the Russian navy; the flagship Knyaz Suvorov is sunk.
src: Wikipedia, History of the Russian Navy

events.t: The Qing dynasty ends in 1912 and a republic follows in China.
RMS Titanic strikes an iceberg in the North Atlantic in April 1912 and sinks with an estimated 2,224 people aboard.

events.n: The First Battle of the Marne
events.t: Germany’s advance on Paris is halted on the Marne in September 1914. The quick victory fails, the war becomes a war on two fronts and the Western Front settles into trenches.
In 1915–1917 the Ottoman Empire destroys its Armenian people, with Assyrians and Greeks, in deportations and massacres.
British, French and ANZAC forces land on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1915; the Ottoman Empire repels them and the campaign is abandoned in 1916.
The Arabs of the Hejaz rise against Ottoman rule in 1916.

events.fig: 57,500 British casualties on the first day
events.t: On 1 July 1916, the first day on the Somme, the British army suffers 57,500 casualties, 19,200 of them dead. By November the battle has cost about 420,000 British, 200,000 French and 500,000 German casualties.
Germany attacks the French positions at Verdun from February to December 1916. The two armies suffer roughly 700,000 to 975,000 casualties, the French more.
Insulin is developed in the early 1920s and roughly triples the life expectancy of diabetics.
Mustafa Kemal abolishes the caliphate in 1924, two years after the Soviet Union adopts state atheism.
John Logie Baird shows the first live working television system in London in 1926, as radio becomes the entertainment of the decade.
A man-made famine kills millions in Soviet Ukraine in 1932–1933.
The Chinese Red Army breaks out of its southern base in 1934 and marches through the west of China to the north in 1934–1935.
In November 1938 the Nazi state unleashes a pogrom against Germany’s Jews.
Japan’s advance across the Pacific is halted at Midway in June 1942, six months after Pearl Harbor.
Enrico Fermi’s reactor achieves the first controlled nuclear chain reaction in 1942. Three years later the bombs fall on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Germany attacks at Kursk on 5 July 1943 and calls the offensive off within a week. The Soviet counter-offensive begins on 12 July and ends German superiority in the east.

events.n: The end of the European empires
events.fig: nearly a billion people in Africa
events.t: In the decades after 1945 decolonisation brings independence to most of Africa and Asia. By the end of the century nearly a billion Africans live in the new nation states.
John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, under William Shockley at Bell Labs, make the first transistor in 1947. The integrated circuit follows in 1958–1959 and the microprocessor, Intel’s 4004, in 1971.
The structure of DNA is determined in 1953, the year of the coronation of Elizabeth II.

The French garrison at Dien Bien Phu surrenders in May 1954, losing about a tenth of French Union manpower in Indochina. The Geneva Accords of July end the French war and divide Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

The war between the communist North and the American-backed South grows after the Gulf of Tonkin in 1964; American strength peaks at 543,400 in April 1969, and the Tet offensive of 1968 strikes more than 100 towns. Between 970,000 and 3 million Vietnamese die, with 58,220 Americans.
Hungarians rise against their Soviet-aligned government in 1956, after the Poznań protests in Poland.
The Great Chinese Famine of 1959–1962 kills tens of millions.
The oral contraceptive pill comes on the market in 1960. Theodore Maiman makes the first working laser the same year.
Israel fights Egypt, Syria and Jordan in the Six-Day War of 1967; Egypt and Syria attack in the Yom Kippur War of 1973.
ARPANET and the British NPL network carry the first packet-switched messages in 1969, on the ideas of Donald Davies and Paul Baran.
The World Health Organization declares smallpox eradicated in 1980, 184 years after Jenner’s first vaccination.
Motorola’s DynaTAC 8000X of 1984 is the first mobile phone on the American market. IBM’s Simon of 1994 is the first smartphone.
The Hubble Space Telescope is launched in 1990.
The CRISPR method of editing genes is dated to 2015 by the timeline of inventions.
Pfizer and BioNTech’s mRNA vaccine against COVID-19 is approved in 2020, the year of the pandemic.

unconfirmed.why: The contract asks for jade and pyrite inlays; the fetched Maya civilization page confirms jade in nobles’ teeth only, so pyrite and the dates are not given.

Only the 16th century BC page was reached, which lists the birth of Zoroaster at c. 1500 BC with no place and no source of its own; his dates are disputed and no second page could be fetched, so the row stands on one tradition.
